intro.heading: Tier is the decision; everything else is detail
paragraphs: Parents at a British-curriculum school in Dubai often arrive at tutoring through a side door. Nobody says 'my child needs Extended-tier Physics support.' They say the grades have slipped, or the science reports have gone from encouraging to careful. Underneath that, nine times out of ten, sits a tiering question: is this pupil being entered for Core or Extended in each science, and does the entry match what the pupil can actually do under timing?

The question matters because tier is a ceiling, not a difficulty setting. A Cambridge IGCSE science entered at Core tier cannot reach the top grades however well the papers are answered. Entered at Extended tier, the full range is available, and the papers contain questions a Core candidate never sees. The decision therefore sets the maximum outcome of two years' work, and it is usually made by a department in Year 10 on the evidence of internal assessments. If that evidence is unrepresentative, the ceiling is set wrongly and nobody notices until results.

The second thing worth understanding is where the marks actually sit. In the Cambridge IGCSE sciences the theory paper is the heavy component, typically half the grade, with the multiple-choice paper at around thirty per cent and the practical or alternative-to-practical component at around twenty. Always check the current syllabus for your child's entry, because Cambridge revises specifications and the live document is the only authority. But the shape tells you something immediately: a pupil losing marks on the twenty-per-cent practical paper and the fifty-per-cent theory paper has two different problems, and they are fixed by two different kinds of session.

This page therefore works subject by subject and paper by paper. It sets out what Core and Extended differ on in Physics 0625, Chemistry 0620 and Biology 0610, where each one leaks marks, what the Alternative to Practical paper really assesses, how the Cambridge route compares with the Pearson Edexcel equivalents, and which Cambridge command terms decide an answer's mark. It also counts the tier decision backwards from the June series, because a tier change has a deadline and a family that discovers the question in April has discovered it too late.

Delivery is stated once and plainly: tuition for Dubai families is one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai, and home visits are a service offered only in India. For a science tier problem that turns out to be an advantage rather than a compromise, because the work is reading a pupil's own marked script together on screen, annotating it, and re-answering the question properly. That is a shared-screen task rather than a kitchen-table one, and it is why the format suits this particular problem so well in practice.

programmes.name: Key Stage 3 science
programmes.description: The three years in which tier allocation is effectively decided. Year 9 internal assessments in physics, chemistry and biology inform the set a pupil is placed into, and a set placement in Year 9 frequently becomes a tier entry in Year 11. programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools stream science from Year 9 in many cases, and a pupil who moves schools within the emirate mid-Key Stage 3 can arrive in a set chosen on another school's evidence. Reconciling that is a short, defined piece of work, and doing it in Year 9 costs a fraction of what recovering a grade ceiling costs in Year 11.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: Two years, a terminal series, and a tier entry per subject. Cambridge offers Core and Extended tiers in the sciences and in mathematics; Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A runs Foundation and Higher. The practical or alternative-to-practical component is examined, not coursework-assessed, which changes how it can be prepared for.

Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, and your child's school knows which zone its timetable comes from.

programmes.name: International A Level sciences
programmes.description: Sixth-form science departments publish IGCSE entry grades, and they apply them. The tier decision made in Year 10 is therefore an admissions decision with a two-year fuse.

Checking those thresholds while your child is in Year 10 turns the tier question into a concrete one: which sciences need Extended entry to keep a sixth-form door open, and what would it take to get there.

dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-for-dubai-english-s.subjectsIntro: Each subject below is given with its Cambridge specification code, the tiers available, and the component where marks most reliably leak. The code matters: Cambridge 0625 and Pearson 4PH1 Physics are not the same examination.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge IGCSE 0625)
subjects.description: Theory paper at around half the grade, multiple choice at around thirty per cent, practical component at twenty. Extended-tier marks leak hardest in extended-response explanation questions and in anything requiring a rearranged equation with units carried through correctly.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge IGCSE 0620)
subjects.description: Moles and organic chemistry decide the Extended-tier grade. A pupil who has not secured mole calculations by the end of Year 10 carries the deficit into every later topic, because titration, yield and electrolysis questions all assume them.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge IGCSE 0610)
subjects.description: High content volume, low conceptual difficulty, which makes it the most self-remediable of the three. Marks go to imprecise terminology and to command-term mismatches far more often than to misunderstanding.

subjects.name: Combined Science (Cambridge IGCSE 0653)
subjects.description: One grade covering all three sciences, with reduced content from each. A sensible entry for a pupil whose strengths are elsewhere, and a constraint on A Level science options, so it is worth checking sixth-form entry rules before the choice is locked.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge IGCSE 0580)
subjects.description: Non-calculator and calculator papers at each tier. Method marks lost in non-calculator working are the commonest avoidable loss, and they respond to a short block of timed practice rather than to re-teaching content.

subjects.name: Physics (Pearson Edexcel 4PH1)
subjects.description: Two written papers with no tiering, so the Core and Extended question does not arise. Pupils transferring between Dubai schools sometimes change board mid-course, and reconciling the two specifications is a defined piece of work rather than a vague worry.

subjects.name: English Language (Cambridge 0500 and 0990)
subjects.description: Reading response and directed writing. The gap is almost always structure under timing rather than vocabulary, and three or four marked scripts with specific rewrite tasks move more than a term of discussion.

subjects.name: Geography (Cambridge IGCSE 0460)
subjects.description: Case-study recall plus skills questions on maps, graphs and photographs. The skills paper is trainable quickly; the case studies are the pupil's own revision work and a tutor's job is to test them, not to supply them.

subjects.name: Computer Science (Cambridge IGCSE 0478)
subjects.description: Algorithm tracing and Cambridge pseudocode conventions decide the paper. Pupils who program confidently in Python often lose marks because the examination wants pseudocode written the Cambridge way.

subjects.name: Arabic as an Additional Language
subjects.description: Sits alongside the Arabic provision every Dubai private school must deliver under KHDA's mandatory-subject requirements, regardless of the licensed curriculum. Script accuracy and reading fluency are the measurable targets.

sections.heading: What Core and Extended actually change on a Cambridge science paper
paragraphs: Core and Extended are not easy and hard versions of the same examination. They are different question papers with different grade ranges, and a pupil sits one or the other. The Core route gives access to the lower part of the grade scale; the Extended route gives access to the whole of it. Once the entry is made, the ceiling is fixed regardless of how well the pupil performs.

The paper structure follows the same logic. In the Cambridge IGCSE sciences, a Core candidate sits the Core multiple-choice paper and the Core theory paper. An Extended candidate sits the Extended versions of both, which contain questions requiring the supplement content and longer written explanation. Both routes sit the same practical or alternative-to-practical component. Always confirm the arrangement on the live syllabus for your child's series, because Cambridge revises specifications and a tutoring page is not the authority on an exam entry.

Where this bites is in the middle of the ability range. A pupil who is comfortable with Core content and shaky on the supplement sits in a genuinely difficult position: Extended entry risks a weaker grade than a strong Core performance, and Core entry closes the top of the scale and often a sixth-form door with it. That decision deserves evidence rather than instinct, and the evidence is a marked Extended-tier script sat under timing. Everything else is an opinion about a child.

One further point parents rarely hear. A department proposing Core entry is usually doing so protectively, on the evidence it has, and it is not wrong to do that. The evidence it has, though, is internal assessment written under classroom conditions, which is not the same instrument as a timed Extended-tier paper. Producing the second instrument costs one or two sessions and gives everyone a better conversation, whichever way it resolves.

sections.heading: Physics 0625: the paper map and where the marks actually go
paragraphs: Physics is the science where understanding and marks diverge most. A pupil can explain to you at the dinner table exactly why a transformer works and still score four out of seven on the question about it, because the mark scheme wants particular physics stated in a particular order with the quantities named. That is a writing problem wearing a physics costume, and it is the single most common thing an Extended-tier Physics tutor is actually paid to fix.

The second recurring loss is equation handling. Extended-tier questions routinely require a formula to be rearranged, a value substituted in non-standard units, and an answer given to a sensible precision with the unit attached. Each of those is a separate opportunity to drop a mark, and a pupil who loses one mark per calculation across a theory paper has lost a grade without getting anything conceptually wrong. Practising this is dull and it works, which is why it tends not to happen without someone insisting.

The third is the practical component. Around a fifth of the grade sits in a paper that asks the candidate to describe a method, identify variables, read instruments, plot and interpret data, and suggest improvements. None of that is about laboratory dexterity, which is why it can be prepared for perfectly well over live video with a shared script on screen. The table below maps the components and names the loss pattern for each.

Reading the table alongside a real script is what makes it useful. Take the pupil's last marked Physics paper, put each lost mark into one of the rows, and the correct purchase becomes obvious rather than arguable. A script with marks scattered across explanation questions needs rewriting practice. A script with marks lost only in the final section needs timed practice. The two look identical on a report and cost very different amounts to fix.

sections.heading: Chemistry 0620: moles and organic decide the Extended grade
paragraphs: Chemistry has a load-bearing topic, and it is the mole. Once a pupil can convert confidently between mass, moles and concentration, a long list of later questions becomes routine: titration calculations, reacting masses, percentage yield, electrolysis quantities. Until they can, every one of those topics has to be guessed at, and the guesses are indistinguishable from a conceptual problem on a report.

The diagnostic is quick. Give the pupil three calculations from an Extended-tier paper and watch what happens in the first thirty seconds. A pupil who starts by writing a balanced equation and identifying what they have been given has secured it. A pupil who starts multiplying numbers has not, and the fix is a short block of work rather than a term of general chemistry support. This is one of the few places where tutoring has a genuinely defined end point.

Organic chemistry is the other. It rewards systematic learning of functional groups, reaction types and naming conventions, and it punishes pupils who have learned examples instead of patterns. The useful session here is not more content delivery; it is making the pupil produce the reaction they have not been shown, from the pattern they have. Both topics, worked properly in Year 10, remove most of the Extended-tier risk in Year 11 and reduce the final-term spend substantially.

Everything else in Chemistry 0620 is more forgiving than its reputation suggests. Bonding, rates of reaction, acids and bases and the periodic table all reward ordinary revision, and a pupil who has moles and organic secured can usually handle them without paid help. Which is why the correct chemistry purchase is narrow and short rather than broad and long: two named topics, a defined number of sessions, and a test at the end that either passes or does not. A chemistry arrangement that runs for four terms without a stated end point has stopped being a repair and become a subscription.

sections.heading: Biology 0610: volume is not the same as difficulty
paragraphs: Biology is the science families most often over-buy. It has the largest content load of the three and the lowest conceptual difficulty, which means a diligent pupil can usually close a biology gap with a revision guide and a schedule. Paying specialist rates for content delivery in biology is one of the commonest ways a tutoring budget is wasted.

What does need another person is precision. Biology mark schemes are unforgiving about terminology: diffusion is not osmosis, a stimulus is not a response, and an answer that says 'the plant grows better' where the mark scheme wants 'the rate of photosynthesis increases' scores nothing despite being broadly right. A pupil cannot usually see this in their own writing, which is exactly what marking is for.

The second thing worth paying for is the command-term discipline shared across all three sciences. 'State' wants a fact and nothing else. 'Describe' wants what happens without explanation. 'Explain' wants a reason, usually with a 'because'. 'Compare' wants both sides in the same sentence. A pupil who writes an explanation for a 'describe' question has written more and scored less, and once that pattern is named it tends to stop within a few weeks. That makes biology the subject where the fewest paid hours produce the most visible movement.

There is one exception worth naming. Biology at Extended tier includes a handful of genuinely demanding areas - genetics problems, the detail of transport in plants, and the quantitative parts of ecology - where a pupil can be diligent and still stuck. Those are legitimate topic purchases of three or four sessions each. The test is whether the pupil can explain the idea back without the book open; if they can, the remaining gap is terminology and timing, and that is marking work rather than teaching work.

sections.heading: The Alternative to Practical paper, and what can be done about it online
paragraphs: Families assume the practical component is the one thing online tuition cannot touch. The opposite is true. The examined paper does not test whether a pupil can set up apparatus; it tests whether they can describe a method precisely, identify independent, dependent and control variables, read a scale to the right precision, tabulate and plot data, draw a line of best fit, interpret it, and suggest a specific improvement. Every one of those is a written skill assessed on paper.

That makes it ideal shared-screen work. A past-paper question is opened on screen, the pupil writes their method, and the tutor marks it live against the mark scheme, showing which clause earned a mark and which was too vague to earn one. 'Measure the temperature' earns nothing; 'measure the temperature of the water every thirty seconds with a thermometer reading to 0.5 degrees Celsius' earns the mark. A pupil typically needs that shown four or five times before it becomes automatic.

Because the component is common to both tiers and all three sciences, a block of work on it is the best-value purchase in the whole science programme. Six to eight sessions on practical paper technique raises marks in Physics, Chemistry and Biology simultaneously, which no amount of single-subject content work can do. The table sets out which skills are examined and how each is trained without a laboratory.

There is one thing the format genuinely cannot replace, and it should be said rather than glossed over. A pupil who has never handled a burette or watched a thermometer settle has a weaker intuition for what a method feels like, and that intuition helps. School laboratory time supplies it, and the tutoring job is to convert that experience into mark-scheme language rather than to substitute for it. Where a school has run a practical, the best session that week is the one that turns it into a written method under timing.

sections.heading: Cambridge against Pearson Edexcel for the same science
paragraphs: Pupils move between Dubai schools, and the schools do not all use the same board. A pupil who has done a year of Cambridge 0625 Physics and transfers to a school entering Pearson 4PH1 has not lost their physics, but they have changed examination. The paper structures differ, the tiering position differs, and revision built round one board's past papers is partly misdirected.

The most consequential difference is tiering. Cambridge offers Core and Extended routes in the sciences; the Pearson International GCSE sciences are single-tier, which removes the ceiling question entirely and raises a different one about whether the pupil can access the whole paper. In mathematics the position reverses in presentation: Cambridge 0580 runs Core and Extended, Pearson 4MA1 runs Foundation and Higher, and the calculator rules are not the same across the two.

The practical answer for a transferring pupil is a short reconciliation exercise rather than a general tutoring arrangement. Establish which board and code the pupil is actually entered for, obtain the right past papers from the official board site, and work through the specification differences topic by topic. That is usually three or four sessions of defined work, and it prevents a term of revision aimed at the wrong examination.

Two practical cautions follow. First, do not trust a subject name alone: a school's prospectus may say 'IGCSE Physics' without naming the board, and the entry form is the only reliable source. Ask the examinations officer for the code. Second, do not buy past papers or specification files from anyone; Cambridge and Pearson publish them on their own sites, and a provider handing over copyrighted material has told you something about how they handle rules generally. Both boards also publish provisional timetables ahead of each series, so the live official document is always the one to work from.

Where a pupil has genuinely studied both boards, there is a small upside nobody mentions. They have seen two question styles on the same physics, and that tends to make the underlying content more robust rather than less. The work is narrowing the practice to the board they will actually sit, not unlearning the other one.

sections.heading: The tier decision, counted backwards from the June series
paragraphs: A tier change has a deadline, and it sits a long way before the paper. Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. The February/March series is offered in India only, so a Dubai family planning round it is planning for a different country. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November.

Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for the centre's zone, warning that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after the wrong zone timetable was used. Ask your child's school which zone it sits in, and work from the live official timetable rather than from any date restated elsewhere. As a guide to how far ahead the machinery runs, the Pearson Edexcel International GCSE November 2026 timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, with results reaching students in January; November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026, and June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026.

Read backwards from the paper, the tier sequence is unforgiving. The evidence that justifies a tier change has to exist before the entry closes, which means the diagnostic needs to happen in the autumn term of Year 11 at the very latest, and ideally in Year 10. By the spring term the entry is made and the only remaining question is how to maximise the grade within the tier already chosen.

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not do with science written work
paragraphs: The honesty line in the sciences is easier to see than in coursework-heavy subjects, and it is worth stating because one page ranking in this market sells completed Internal Assessments outright. A tutor teaches, questions, models and marks. A tutor does not produce the pupil's work, supply paragraphs, or write a method the pupil then submits as their own.

In practice that means the useful session looks like this. The pupil writes an answer. The tutor marks it against the mark scheme and says which clause earned a mark and which did not. The pupil rewrites it. The tutor marks it again. Nothing in that loop requires the tutor to write anything the pupil submits, and the pupil ends up with a skill rather than a product. Where a school practical write-up is assessed internally, the same rule applies with more force: feedback on the pupil's draft is legitimate; supplying the content is not.

The same restraint applies to material. Cambridge and Pearson own their syllabuses, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables, and the right behaviour is to link the official page rather than hand over files. IB Gram holds no KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, MoE, Cambridge, Pearson or IB approval, accreditation or partnership and makes no such claim. It is an online matching platform with no premises in the UAE, and anyone describing tutors as approved by a UAE regulator is describing something that does not exist.

Worth adding, because it cuts the other way: holding this line is a service rather than a restriction. A pupil who submits work a tutor wrote has exposed their whole qualification to a malpractice finding, and the risk sits with the candidate, not the provider who took the fee. Parents are entitled to ask a prospective tutor, plainly, what they would do if asked to write a paragraph. The answer tells you more than any qualification on a profile.

sections.heading: Coverage, scheduling and the first session
paragraphs: Extended-tier Physics, Chemistry, Biology and Mathematics are the best-covered subjects in this set, and a match is usually quick. Minority combinations are thinner. A pupil needing Extended-tier Computer Science 0478 with Cambridge pseudocode conventions, Arabic as a first language, or a specific Pearson science code mid-transfer may wait longer, and in a given week the honest answer may be that nobody suitable is free.

Three outcomes are possible and a family should be told which applies. The subject is covered and a trial lesson is scheduled within a few days. The subject is covered by a specialist working into Gulf Standard Time from outside the UAE, which is disclosed rather than concealed behind a local-looking telephone number. Or the subject is not currently covered at the tier required, in which case saying so is better than placing a generalist and invoicing for the gap.

Scheduling is the practical constraint for a Dubai family rather than geography. Pupils in Silicon Oasis are home by four; pupils in Mudon or Nad Al Sheba are not home until well after five. A slot fifteen minutes after your child actually walks in survives the term; a slot fifteen minutes after the bell does not. The first session is free, is one session, and requires no card details, which exists so a tiering judgement can be tested before anything is spent.

Two more scheduling notes specific to a Dubai school year. Revision for the June series runs through the spring term, which in some years overlaps Ramadan; moving sessions to a post-Iftar slot keeps the most valuable quarter of the two-year course intact, where pausing for six weeks does not. And the summer gap is long. A pupil going into Year 11 with a known topic gap is better served by four sessions in August than by twelve in February, because the content is still available to be fixed rather than merely revised.

process.title: Establish the code and the tier
process.description: Find out exactly which specification each science is being taught to and which tier the pupil is provisionally entered for. Cambridge 0625 and Pearson 4PH1 are different examinations, and Core and Extended are different papers. A tutor working from the wrong one is wasting your money politely and consistently.

process.title: Get a timed Extended-tier script marked
process.description: Have the pupil sit Extended-tier questions under examination timing and have the script marked against the real mark scheme. This is the only evidence that answers the tier question. Internal assessment grades tell you a position; a marked script tells you whether the pupil can reach the supplement content.

process.title: Separate the content gap from the writing gap
process.description: Sort the lost marks into content not known, method not shown, command term misread and time run out. Each has a different cost and a different fix. A pupil losing explanation marks needs rewriting practice, not re-teaching, and the two are frequently confused at the point of purchase.

process.title: Buy the practical component once, for all three sciences
process.description: Six to eight sessions on practical paper technique raises marks in Physics, Chemistry and Biology at the same time, because the same skills are examined in each. It is the best-value block in the programme and it is routinely skipped in favour of single-subject content work.

process.title: Fix a slot that survives the commute
process.description: Choose a start time fifteen minutes after your child is actually home, not after the bell. Silicon Oasis pupils can do 4.30pm; Mudon and Nad Al Sheba pupils realistically cannot. Online delivery means the late slot costs no travel surcharge and carries no traffic cancellation risk.

whyPoints.title: Specification codes, not subject names
whyPoints.description: Matching starts from the code and tier printed on your child's exam entry: 0625 or 4PH1, Core or Extended, 0580 or 4MA1. Every session is then built from the school's own scheme of work, so the pupil is never revising content their class has not reached or has already left behind.

whyPoints.title: Marks explained, not difficulty discussed
whyPoints.description: The work is reading your child's own marked script and naming where the marks went: content, method, command term or timing. Those four categories have different costs and different fixes, and a page that only talks about subjects being hard cannot help you choose between them.

whyPoints.title: The practical paper taken seriously
whyPoints.description: Around a fifth of each Cambridge science grade sits in a component that tests written method, variables and data handling rather than laboratory skill. It is fully trainable on a shared screen and it pays across all three sciences at once, which makes it the most under-bought block in the market.

whyPoints.title: Tier evidence a school can read
whyPoints.description: A tier conversation goes better with a timed, marked Extended-tier script than with a parent's concern. The output of a diagnostic is a written note naming the topics, the mark categories and the realistic ceiling, in a form a head of science can act on.

whyPoints.title: Delivery and coverage stated plainly
whyPoints.description: Lessons are one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai; home visits are an India-only service. Where a minority subject or tier has no specialist free, that is disclosed rather than filled with a generalist.

whyPoints.title: No claim that cannot be evidenced
whyPoints.description: No grade promises, no satisfaction percentages, no self-asserted ratings, and no suggestion that KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, MoE, Cambridge, Pearson or the IB has approved, accredited or partnered with IB Gram. Board documents are linked at source rather than reproduced.

faqs.question: What do Core and Extended tier actually mean for a Dubai English Speaking College science pupil?
faqs.answer: They are two different question papers with two different grade ranges, not an easy and a hard version of one examination. A Core entry gives access to the lower part of the grade scale and cannot reach the top grades however well the pupil performs. An Extended entry opens the whole scale and includes supplement content and longer written explanation questions. Both routes sit the same practical or alternative-to-practical component. The entry is usually proposed by the science department during Year 10, which makes Year 10 the point at which a marginal case is worth evidencing properly.

faqs.question: Can a pupil move from Core to Extended tier partway through Year 11?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and the deadline is earlier than most families expect. The entry is made by the centre months before the paper is sat, so any evidence that justifies a change has to exist before that point. In practice the useful window is the autumn term of Year 11 at the latest. What persuades a department is not a parent's concern but a timed Extended-tier script marked against the real mark scheme, showing the pupil reaching supplement content. Ask the school directly what evidence it wants and when its internal deadline falls.

faqs.question: Which of the three Cambridge sciences leaks the most marks at Extended tier?
faqs.answer: Physics, by a clear margin, and usually for a writing reason rather than a physics one. Extended-tier theory papers ask for explanation in a particular order with quantities named, and a pupil who can explain a transformer out loud can still score four out of seven for it. Equation handling is the second loss: rearranging, substituting in non-standard units, and giving a sensible precision with the unit attached are three separate chances to drop a mark. Both are trainable by rewriting the pupil's own answers against the mark scheme rather than by more content teaching.

faqs.question: How is the Alternative to Practical paper marked, and can it be practised over video?
faqs.answer: It is marked on written precision, not laboratory skill. The paper asks the candidate to describe a method with quantities, instruments and intervals stated, identify independent, dependent and control variables, read scales to the correct precision, tabulate and plot data, interpret a trend, and suggest a specific improvement. All of that is written work on paper, which makes it ideal shared-screen practice: the pupil writes, the tutor marks it live against the mark scheme, and the pupil rewrites. 'Measure the temperature' earns nothing; the version with a thermometer, a precision and an interval earns the mark.

faqs.question: My child understands circuits but cannot write a six-mark explanation. Is that fixable?
faqs.answer: Yes, and relatively quickly, because it is a writing problem rather than a physics one. The mark scheme for an extended-response question allocates a mark per idea, in a sequence, with the relevant quantities named. A pupil who writes a fluent paragraph that mentions four of the six ideas scores four. The fix is mechanical: the pupil writes the answer, the tutor marks it clause by clause showing which earned a mark, the pupil rewrites it, and the loop repeats. Most pupils internalise the shape after four or five questions handled that way.

faqs.question: What changes if my child transfers from Cambridge 0625 Physics to Pearson 4PH1?
faqs.answer: The physics travels with them; the examination does not. The Cambridge IGCSE sciences run Core and Extended tiers, while the Pearson International GCSE sciences are single-tier, so the ceiling question disappears and a different one appears about accessing the whole paper. Paper structures and question styles differ, and revision built round the wrong board's past papers is partly misdirected. The sensible response is a short reconciliation exercise of three or four sessions: confirm the code on the entry, get the right official past papers, and work the specification differences topic by topic.

faqs.question: How much of Chemistry 0620 actually depends on getting moles right?
faqs.answer: More than any other single topic. Once mole calculations are secure, titrations, reacting masses, percentage yield and electrolysis quantities all become routine; until they are, every one of those has to be guessed at, and on a report that looks like a general chemistry weakness. The diagnostic takes two minutes: give three Extended-tier calculations and watch the first thirty seconds. A pupil who writes the balanced equation first has secured it. A pupil who starts multiplying numbers has not, and the fix is a short defined block rather than a term of broad support.

faqs.question: Does Biology 0610 need fewer paid hours than Physics or Chemistry?
faqs.answer: Usually, yes, and families routinely over-buy it. Biology has the largest content load of the three sciences and the lowest conceptual difficulty, so a diligent pupil can often close a content gap with a revision guide and a schedule rather than with a specialist. What does need another reader is terminology precision: diffusion is not osmosis, and 'the plant grows better' scores nothing where the mark scheme wants 'the rate of photosynthesis increases'. Pupils cannot see that in their own writing, which is what marking is for, and it moves quickly once named.

faqs.question: What do the Cambridge command terms state, describe and explain each require?
faqs.answer: They are instructions about how much to write, and ignoring them costs marks while writing more. 'State' wants a fact and nothing else, so an added reason earns nothing and uses time. 'Describe' wants what happens, with no causal account. 'Explain' wants a reason, usually signalled by 'because'. 'Compare' wants both sides addressed in the same answer rather than two separate paragraphs. 'Suggest' invites applying known science to an unfamiliar context. A pupil who writes explanations for describe questions is working harder for fewer marks, and naming the pattern usually stops it within weeks.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with a school science practical write-up?
faqs.answer: A tutor can give feedback on the pupil's own draft and teach the skills the write-up needs. A tutor cannot write it, supply paragraphs for it, or edit it to completion, and no price makes that acceptable. Where a write-up contributes to an internally assessed mark, the rule tightens rather than loosens, because the mark has to represent the pupil's own work. The legitimate loop is simple: the pupil writes, the tutor marks against the criteria and names what is missing, the pupil rewrites. One page in this market sells finished coursework outright, which is a malpractice risk rather than a service.

faqs.question: When is the latest useful point to start science tutoring before the June series?
faqs.answer: For technique work, eight to twelve weeks before the paper is still a genuinely productive window, because timed practice with marking and re-answering moves marks right up to study leave. For a content gap spanning a third of the specification, that window is too late and the honest advice is to protect the subjects that can still move. For a tier question it is far too late, because the entry closed months earlier. The ordering matters: tier decisions belong in Year 10, content repair in the autumn of Year 11, technique in the final quarter.

faqs.question: Does the November series work as a resit route for a single science?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is a normal plan rather than a failure plan. Cambridge runs IGCSE examinations in a June series and a November series, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. The February/March series is offered in India only and is irrelevant to a UAE candidate. As a guide to the timing, the Pearson November 2026 timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026 with results reaching students in January; November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Entries go through the centre, so start with your child's examinations officer.

faqs.question: Do you send tutors to Academic City, Mirdif or Al Warqa addresses?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; sending a tutor to a family's address is a service offered only in India. Tutoring for Dubai families is delivered one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time. For a science tier problem that is an advantage rather than a compromise: the work is reading a marked script together on screen, annotating it and re-answering the question, which is shared-screen work. It also means the tutor is chosen for the specification and tier rather than for living within driving distance of your community.

faqs.question: How many sessions does a single science topic gap usually take?
faqs.answer: It depends which of four things is wrong, and the diagnostic is worth doing before buying a term. A timing gap, where the content is known and the paper is not finished, typically closes in four or five sessions of timed practice. A technique gap, where marks are lost to command terms or missing method, takes six to ten. A genuine topic gap, such as moles never secured, takes about a term. A foundation gap, where the pupil cannot access the tier at all, is a school conversation about entry before anyone is paid anything.

A free trial lesson is one session with no card details required, so the judgement can be tested before anything is spent. Lessons are one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, and any subject or tier not currently covered will be named rather than filled with a generalist.

dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-for-dubai-heights-a.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE across mathematics, the sciences and the essay subjects, one-to-one over live video. Every arrangement reports progress in a form that can be set beside the school's own data rather than instead of it.

intro.heading: Three sources, none of which agrees with the others
paragraphs: A Dubai parent in Year 10 or 11 is not short of information about their child. There is a termly report with effort and attainment grades. There is a predicted or target grade, arrived at by a method nobody has explained. There is a set placement that was decided at some point on evidence nobody has shown. There is a KHDA inspection band for the school. And there is the child's own account, which is usually more pessimistic than the reports and more optimistic than the mocks.

The trouble is that these five sources measure quite different things, and they are frequently read as though they all measured the same thing. A KHDA band describes a school's provision across the whole institution. A report attainment grade describes a teacher's judgement of current standard against a curriculum expectation. A predicted grade is a forecast made for a purpose, often an administrative one. A mock result is one performance on one paper. None is wrong; each answers a different question, and treating them as a single noisy signal is how families end up buying a term of tutoring aimed at nothing in particular.

This matters at a school with a growing secondary phase in particular, because the institutional machinery is still settling. A department running its second or third IGCSE cohort has less historical data to calibrate predictions against than one running its fifteenth, which makes predicted grades genuinely harder to produce accurately. That is not a criticism; it is a reason for a parent to ask how a prediction was made rather than to accept or dispute the number.

The approach that works is triangulation. Take the school's data, take one independent measurement using the same instrument the examination uses, and take the pupil's own account of which questions they can and cannot do. Where all three agree, you have a fact and you can act on it. Where two agree and one does not, the odd one out is usually explainable, and the explanation is itself informative. Where all three disagree, nobody should be spending money until somebody has read a script.

So this page is about reading what you already have before buying anything new. What a KHDA inspection report does and does not tell you about your own child. What each report in the school year is for. Who makes a predicted grade and on what basis. The questions at parents' evening that produce facts. And what to do when the school's view and your own measurement part company. Tuition for Dubai families is one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai, and home visits are a service offered only in India.

dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-for-dubai-heights-a.programmesIntro: The school's reporting machinery changes as a pupil moves up, and so does what is worth asking. Below is what each stage actually produces and what to make of it.

programmes.name: Key Stage 3
programmes.description: Reports at this stage carry curriculum-expectation judgements rather than grade predictions, which makes them harder to compare across schools and easier to read within one. The most consequential data point is the set placement, because in most Dubai schools the set a pupil occupies at the end of Year 9 informs the IGCSE tier a department later proposes.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools vary considerably in how often they review sets, and a pupil who moves into the emirate mid-Key Stage 3 may be placed on another school's evidence without reconciliation. Asking what triggers a set review is a reasonable question and the answer is a useful piece of information about the department.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: The best-documented stage, because external instruments exist. Reports carry working-at grades, mocks produce marked scripts, and predicted grades are made for sixth-form applications. Every one of these can be compared against a board past paper marked to the published scheme, which is the only genuinely external measurement available.
programmes.countryNote: UAE candidates sit June and November. The mock season is the most useful fixed point in a Dubai school year for a parent, because it produces a marked script under conditions somebody else arranged. Asking for the script rather than the grade is the highest-return request available.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Reporting shifts from paper marks to criterion letters, because internal assessments are scored against lettered criteria with stated mark allocations. That is more informative than a grade if a parent knows to ask for it, since a draft can be scored criterion by criterion rather than discussed in general terms.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai keeps adding Diploma places, with three of the seven schools joining the 2026-27 intake offering the International Baccalaureate among 16,846 new places. For a family moving up from IGCSE, the shift is from asking about marks to asking which criterion is unmet and why.

programmes.name: International A Level
programmes.description: Predicted grades become load-bearing here, because university applications depend on them. The method behind a prediction therefore stops being an academic curiosity and becomes something worth understanding precisely, including what evidence the department uses and at what point in the year it is fixed.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai sixth forms publish their own entry grades for their courses, which gives a Year 11 family a numeric target. That target is the single most useful piece of measurement infrastructure in the system, and it should be looked up rather than inferred from a conversation.

dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-for-dubai-heights-a.subjectsIntro: Each subject below is listed with the school data point that actually carries information about it, because the right question differs by subject. Asking about effort in mathematics tells you almost nothing.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge IGCSE 0580)
subjects.description: Ask about the tier of entry and the mock script, not about effort. Tier caps the grade, and a marked script separates method losses from content losses. Those two facts tell you more than a year of reports.

subjects.name: Mathematics A (Pearson Edexcel 4MA1)
subjects.description: Ask which specification code is on the entry, because a school running both boards across year groups creates genuine confusion. Practice aimed at the wrong code is the most common silent waste in a tutoring arrangement.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge IGCSE 0625)
subjects.description: Ask for the theory and practical component marks separately. A single physics grade conceals the common pattern of a pupil improving on explanation questions while flat on written method, and they need different work.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge IGCSE 0620)
subjects.description: Ask whether mole calculations are secure, as a yes or no. It is a binary question with a two-minute test, and it is more informative than any attainment grade the subject will generate all year.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge IGCSE 0610)
subjects.description: Ask whether marks are being lost to terminology or to content. Biology reports often say 'needs more detail', which covers both and distinguishes neither, and the two repairs differ in length by a factor of several.

subjects.name: First Language English (Cambridge 0500 and 0990)
subjects.description: Ask which assessment objective is weakest. A report saying 'writes fluently' alongside a static grade means the objectives being missed are not language ones, and the teacher usually knows exactly which they are.

subjects.name: Literature in English (Cambridge 0475 and 0992)
subjects.description: Ask for the set text list and the component structure in writing. Literature support aimed at a text the school did not choose is wasted entirely, and the list changes over time.

subjects.name: History (Cambridge IGCSE 0470)
subjects.description: Ask how source questions are scoring against essay questions. The two use different skills and a combined grade hides which half is failing, which is the whole of the diagnosis in this subject.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Studies
subjects.description: Ask for data-response marks separately from evaluation marks. A pupil who knows every definition and loses the entire evaluation allocation has a specific, cheap and completely invisible problem on a report.

subjects.name: Arabic as an Additional Language
subjects.description: Runs alongside the Arabic provision Dubai private schools must deliver under KHDA's mandatory-subject requirements, whatever the licensed curriculum. Progress is measurable week to week, which makes it easy to verify independently.

dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-for-dubai-heights-a.regionsTitle: The Al Barsha South and Arjan communities this page serves
dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-for-dubai-heights-a.regionsIntro: A school in the Al Barsha South corridor draws from a ring of apartment and villa communities along the Umm Suqeim and Al Khail arterials. The relevant fact for a measurement plan is when a pupil can sit a paper properly without the day already having gone.

regions.name: Al Barsha South
regions.note: Immediately around the corridor, so pupils are often home within twenty minutes. A weekday timed paper is realistic here, which matters because a script produced at eight in the evening understates what a pupil can do.

regions.name: Arjan and Dubailand Residences
regions.note: Apartment-dense and close enough that children are back early, though the internal road network is slower than it looks on a map. Early-evening sessions work well for marking and rewriting rather than fresh timed work.

regions.name: Dubai Hills Estate
regions.note: Slow on the Al Khail approach at school-run time, pushing most households to a 5.30pm start or later. Full papers are better sat at a weekend here, when the comparison with earlier attempts stays meaningful.

regions.name: Al Barsha 1, 2 and 3
regions.note: Established, mixed-density districts with short runs to the corridor. Families here frequently have children at two different schools, which makes a single fixed weekly slot per child more valuable than a flexible arrangement.

regions.name: Motor City and Sports City
regions.note: Well supplied with tuition centres, so group classes at roughly AED 100-150 per pupil are easy to find. Group work cannot produce an individual marked script, which is the thing a measurement plan actually needs.

regions.name: Jumeirah Village Circle
regions.note: The largest single source of enquiries in this corridor and generally on a tighter education budget, which is where the AED 45-150 online band finds its market. At Extended tier the difference shows in extended-response marks.

regions.name: Al Quoz and Al Khail Heights
regions.note: Short distances with awkward peak congestion. Pupils are usually home by five, and a session at that hour is fine for reviewing a script and poor for sitting a new one under timing.

schoolClusters.city: The Al Barsha South, Arjan and Dubai Hills corridor
schoolClusters.note: A dense cluster of British-curriculum and IB schools, several with secondary phases still filling. A department running its second or third IGCSE cohort has less historical data to calibrate predictions against, which is a reason to ask how a prediction was made.

schoolClusters.city: The Motor City, Sports City and JVC belt
schoolClusters.note: Schools at a wide range of fee levels within a short radius, which means pupils transfer between them regularly. A transferring pupil arrives with another school's assessment history and no reconciliation, so a fresh independent measurement matters more than usual.

modes.title: A triangulation session, one or two hours
modes.description: Bring the last two reports, the predicted grade, the mock script and your child's own account. The session reconciles them: which sources agree, which do not, and what the disagreement means. The output is a short written note naming the one thing worth working on and the questions worth asking the school.

modes.description: An hour a week on the identified target, with a short written note each month that uses the same language the school uses: working-at grade, marks on named question types, and the component where the movement is or is not happening. A note the department can read is worth more than a longer one it cannot.

sections.heading: What a KHDA inspection report tells you about your own child
paragraphs: Almost nothing, and that is worth saying plainly because inspection bands drive an enormous amount of Dubai parental decision-making. KHDA inspects Dubai private schools annually and rates them on a six-band scale from Outstanding down to Very Weak. The judgement describes institutional provision: teaching quality across the school, leadership, curriculum, safeguarding, inclusion, the progress of cohorts. It is a statement about a school, aggregated across hundreds of pupils.

An individual child's trajectory is not derivable from it in either direction. A pupil can be under-served in a specific subject at an Outstanding school, because a band is an average across departments and one department can be weaker than the rest. Equally a pupil can be extremely well taught in one subject at a school rated lower overall. The band is genuinely useful when choosing between schools and genuinely useless when diagnosing one child's stuck grade.

What an inspection report does contain, and what almost nobody reads, is subject-level and phase-level commentary. The narrative sections often identify specific strengths and weaknesses by subject and key stage, and that is information a parent can use: if a report notes that attainment in a particular subject in the secondary phase is weaker than elsewhere, and your child's stuck grade is in that subject, the two facts belong in the same conversation with the school.

The reasonable use of the band, then, is as context rather than as evidence. Dubai's market is deep: KHDA counted 387,441 pupils across 227 private schools offering seventeen different curricula in 2024-25, with seven more schools joining the 2026-27 intake creating 16,846 places. In a market that size, bands help with selection. They do not substitute for a marked script, and no amount of institutional quality tells you which questions your child lost marks on last month.

sections.heading: The reporting cycle, and what each report is actually for
paragraphs: A Dubai school year produces several documents and they are not interchangeable. An early-year baseline or settling report describes a starting position and is often based on limited evidence, which makes it a poor instrument for anything but spotting an obvious mismatch. A mid-year full report carries the most considered teacher judgement of the year, because it sits after a term of work and usually after an internal assessment series.

A mock report is a different animal again. It reports performance on a specific paper under specific conditions, and its usefulness depends entirely on what those conditions were: whether the syllabus was complete, whether it was sat under examination conditions, and whether the marking was calibrated to board standards or deliberately harsh. Those three questions turn a mock grade from a verdict into a measurement, and all three are answerable by asking.

End-of-year reports in Year 10 are the most actionable document a family receives, because they arrive with a whole year still available and before any entry is fixed. A Year 10 report showing a subject below where it needs to be leaves time for content repair over the summer, which is the cheapest and most effective window in the sequence. The same information in a Year 11 spring report leaves only triage.

What to do with each report is therefore different. The baseline is for spotting mismatches. The mid-year report is for identifying the one subject worth working on. The mock is for reading the script. The end-of-year Year 10 report is for planning a summer. Reading all four with the same question - is this good or bad - extracts a fraction of the information each contains.

sections.heading: Predicted grades: who makes them, how, and what for
paragraphs: A predicted grade is a forecast made by a teacher or department for a purpose, and the purpose shapes the number. A prediction for a sixth-form application is a different artefact from a prediction for internal tracking, and a prediction given to a parent to prompt effort is different again. Asking what this particular prediction is for is not a cynical question; it is the question that makes the number interpretable.

The method matters more than the number. A prediction built from a pupil's performance on board past papers marked to the published scheme is a measurement. A prediction built from classwork, effort and a teacher's experience of similar pupils is a judgement, and often a good one, but it is calibrated against that teacher's own cohort history. In a department running its second or third IGCSE cohort there is less of that history to calibrate against, which is a structural fact rather than a failing.

Predictions also have a fixing point, and parents rarely know when it is. Before it, a prediction can move on new evidence. After it, especially where it has gone into an application, it is effectively settled. Knowing that date changes what is worth doing: producing evidence a fortnight before the fixing point is useful, and producing the same evidence a fortnight after it is not.

The useful posture is neither accepting nor disputing the number but asking how it was built. Which assessments contributed. Whether any board past paper was involved. What the pupil would need to demonstrate for it to move. Departments generally answer those questions straightforwardly, and the answers tell you whether a prediction is a measurement to be worked with or a judgement to be supplemented with one.

sections.heading: The parents' evening questions that produce information
paragraphs: Parents' evenings produce reassurance because the questions invite it. 'How is she doing?' has one realistic answer in a five-minute slot, and it is a positive summary. A different set of questions produces facts, and teachers generally answer them willingly because they are answerable and specific rather than evaluative. The shift is from asking for a verdict to asking for data.

The questions that work share a shape: they name a component, a question type or an evidence source. Which component is costing the most marks. What was the split between method losses and content losses on the mock. Which tier is my child provisionally entered for, and what would change that. Which specification code are we working to. Is the Alternative to Practical paper stronger or weaker than the theory papers. What is the one thing you would have her practise this term.

The last of those is disproportionately useful. A subject teacher who sees a pupil several times a week usually has a precise answer, and it is almost never 'work harder'. It is something like 'she needs to write the method out even when she can see the answer' or 'she needs to stop writing explanations for describe questions'. That sentence is a tutoring brief, produced free, by the person with the most information.

There is a question not to ask, or at least not to lead with. Asking whether a child needs a tutor puts a teacher in an awkward position and rarely produces a useful answer. Asking what the pupil needs to practise produces the same information without the awkwardness, and leaves the decision about who supervises that practice where it belongs, which is with the family.

sections.heading: Triangulating three sources before spending anything
paragraphs: Three independent sources exist and they cost nothing to assemble. The school's data: reports, set placement, predicted grade, mock script. One independent measurement: a board past paper, downloaded from the official Cambridge or Pearson site, sat under timing and marked against the published scheme. And the pupil's own account of which questions they can and cannot do, which is more reliable than parents expect and more pessimistic than reports.

Where all three agree, that is a fact and it should be acted on without further investigation. A report saying detail is missing, a script showing explanation marks lost, and a pupil saying they never know how much to write on the long questions is a single diagnosis arriving by three routes. The work is obvious, narrow and cheap, and no further diagnosis is needed before starting.

Where two agree and one does not, the odd one out usually has an explanation worth having. A strong report with a weak script often means the internal assessment was easier or less time-pressured than a board paper. A weak report with a strong script sometimes means the pupil performs under pressure and coasts otherwise. A pupil's account that contradicts both is sometimes anxiety and sometimes information nobody else has.

Where all three disagree, nobody should be buying anything yet. That pattern usually means one of the instruments is broken: a mock marked to an uncalibrated standard, a report based on thin evidence, or a past paper from the wrong specification. Checking which instrument is faulty costs an hour and prevents a term of misdirected work, and that hour is the single best-value thing in this entire page.

sections.heading: What progress should look like between two reports
paragraphs: School reports arrive at intervals of roughly a term, which is a long time to wait for a signal. If tutoring begins after a mid-year report, the next school data point is months away, and in the meantime something has to indicate whether the work is landing. That something has to be produced deliberately, because nothing in the school calendar will produce it.

At four weeks the indicator is behavioural rather than numeric. The thing being targeted should be visible in the pupil's written work: method written out, the analysis sentence present, units attached, the question re-read before answering. Marks may not have moved and that is normal over four weeks. What is not normal is nothing at all having been produced that could be looked at.

At eight weeks the indicator should be numeric and narrow. Marks on the specific question types being worked on, compared against the baseline, under the same conditions. Not the overall grade, which is noisy over eight weeks and influenced by which topics happened to be on the paper. If the targeted marks have not moved, the diagnosis, the match or the between-session work is wrong, and all three are findable.

By the next school report there should be agreement, and the agreement is the real test. A school report that reflects the movement your own measurement showed means the work is landing in the classroom and not only in the sessions. A report that does not reflect it means either the movement is narrower than it looked or the teacher is measuring something else, and that discrepancy is worth raising rather than ignoring.

sections.heading: When the school's view and your measurement disagree
paragraphs: This happens often and it is not usually anyone's fault. Schools and board papers measure different things under different conditions, and the gap between an internal assessment and a Cambridge or Pearson paper is real. An internal test is written to assess what has just been taught; a board paper assesses the whole specification with unfamiliar contexts and tighter timing. A pupil can be genuinely good at the first and genuinely weaker at the second.

The productive response is to treat the disagreement as information rather than as a dispute. If your independent measurement is substantially lower than the school's view, the likely explanations are specification coverage, timing pressure or unfamiliar question styles, and each suggests a different piece of work. If it is substantially higher, the likely explanation is that the pupil performs better under pressure than in class, which is a different and more pleasant problem.

Bringing it to the school works better than it sounds, provided it is brought as evidence rather than as a challenge. A timed board past paper, marked against the published scheme, with lost marks categorised, speaks the department's own language and asks nothing to be taken on trust. A head of department can read it in five minutes. A parental impression, however accurate, cannot be acted on in the same way.

Timing again determines what can happen. A discrepancy raised in the autumn of Year 11 can still influence a tier entry; the same discrepancy raised in March cannot, because the entry has closed. The general principle is to produce evidence a full term before the decision it is meant to influence, and to ask the department directly what evidence it would find persuasive, which is a disarming question that usually gets a straight answer.
